newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Organised crime threatens Bulgarian state - premier.
newsitem.headline: Organised crime threatens Bulgarian state - premier.

text.p: Prime Minister Ivan Kostov said on Tuesday organised crime threatened to destroy state authority in Bulgaria and had virtually replaced it in some parts of the formerly communist country.
"There is a threat to the functioning of the state as in some regions organised criminal groupings are behaving as official state authorities," Kostov told a news conference.
He said his ruling Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) was launching a campaign to restore confidence in the state, whose weakness he blamed on his Socialist predecessors.

"The state has been weakening through organised crime in the last several years and we have found a really heavily damaged state administration and institutions," said Kostov, whose government took office in May.

Numerous shady groupings sprang up in the legal and administrative chaos which followed the collapse of four decades of one-party rule in 1989. The UDF has made the fight against organised crime and corruption a priority.
As well as home-grown crime, Interior Ministry Secretary Bozidar Popov told Reuters that Russian mafia were operating in Bulgaria with the help of local criminal groups.

"They operate on different levels -- crime on roads, in streets and tourist complexes and some of their more organised operations are using Bulgarian frontmen to buy estates and hotels," Popov told Reuters.

He said Russian criminal groups had been involved in drug trafficking but dealt mostly with trafficking in women via Bulgaria, who go to work as prostitutes in Europe and neighbouring Greece and Turkey.
He said the groups also included citizens of former Soviet republics such as Ukraine, Georgia and Chechnya.
Last month, Bulgaria's cabinet approved amendments to the penal and criminal codes to speed up legal procedure and improve the legislative basis for fighting organised crime.
All parliamentary parties gave their support in principle to the campaign, but the Prosecutor's Office has said some of the draft texts violated people's constitutional rights.
Chief Prosecutor Ivan Tatarchev said on Tuesday the changes were too hasty and urged a wider discussion among experts.
Kostov said he hoped that the amendments would be passed by parliament by the end of July, before the summer recess.
He said UDF leaders would travel around the country to explain the measures being introduced by the government.
"Our aim is to get the people on our side, to convince them there will be nothing to fear as they would be protected by the legislation and the official state authority."
